newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Baker seen reviving Western Sahara peace effort.
newsitem.headline: Baker seen reviving Western Sahara peace effort.

text.p: U.N. special envoy James Baker's four-day diplomatic foray into North Africa has breathed new life into the stalled peace process in the disputed territory of Western Sahara, diplomats said.

During the former U.S. secretary of state's last stop at a refugee camp in western Algeria on Sunday, the Polisario Front, which seeks independence for the former Spanish colony claimed by Morocco, said it was freeing 85 Moroccan prisoners of war.

Baker hailed the release of soldiers captured during the war between the Polisario movement and Morocco from 1976 to 1991 as a "very, very generous humanitarian gesture". A ceasefire brokered by the United Nations has been in effect for the past six years.

Diplomatic sources and aid workers in the desert village of Tindouf, Polisario's base in Algeria, welcomed the release as tangible evidence of progress in Baker's whirlwind visits to Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania and the Polisario camps.

The sources said there were other signs that Baker's U.N. mission could finally solve the two-decade-old conflict that has been a running sore in relations between Algeria, which backs the Polisario, and the neighbouring kingdom of Morocco.

For one, Baker is seen as a fair, high-profile negotiator whose diplomacy in the 1991 Gulf War and the Middle East showed a level of finesse observers say will be needed to find a solution in Western Sahara that is acceptable to all parties.
Baker's convoy was greeted on Sunday by tens of thousands of cheering refugees at Smara camp in the harsh Hamada desert.
Their homeland is a mass of sand in northwestern Africa that has rich deposits of phosphates and 1,500 km (940 miles) of Atlantic coastline with lucrative fishing rights.

"You have to have a heavyweight to try to solve this situation...from a country that has an interest, but not a particular interest, in the region," said a U.N. official who spoke to Reuters on condition of anonymity.
All parties to the conflict are clearly unhappy with the status quo, leading U.N. officials to conclude the time may be ripe for a resolution.

"I am convinced that the people in this region are overly weary with this issue and this problem and are ready for a just, lasting and definitive solution," Baker told a news conference on Sunday after meeting Polisario leaders in the Smara camp.
By appointing an American, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan also focused international attention on a conflict that could destabilise a sensitive region at NATO's southern flank.

The 1991 ceasefire, monitored by about 240 U.N. military observers and support staff, called for a referendum on the status of the area -- independence or integration with Morocco. But it was repeatedly delayed over dispute on who could vote and was finally abandoned in 1995.

Algeria has provided political and diplomatic backing as well as arms to the Polisario Front, but now wants to ease friction and strengthen trade ties with Morocco through the Arab Maghreb Union, a North African trade bloc, a U.N. official said.
According to Polisario, some 170,000 refugees live in the bleak camps, situated in an inhospitable stretch of the Sahara just inside western Algeria.
They are mostly nomads who fled the Western Sahara in the mid-1970s when Morocco moved in as the Spaniards left.
A generation of children has grown up in the vast camps suffering malnutrition, dysentery and other health problems related to foul water supplies and harsh desert conditions.

Aid workers privately say that the Polisario, which controls the camps through the self-proclaimed Arab Sahara Democratic Republic, see the camps as a way of keeping up international pressure for a settlement.

The real worry remains that the Polisario will make good on a threat to restart the war, where they proved to be excellent desert fighters in the battle against Morocco's larger and better-equipped military.

"We are ready to return to war if the Moroccans don't leave our country," Abdurah Aman, a squad leader fighting since 1975, said. "If we are here to get independence and if we've lost our mothers, fathers and brothers, it's not for any other reason."
